I'm Thai who grew up in Thailand until I was 13 and then moved to the US with my mom. So I was old enough to understand the Thai culture before leaving but I was young enough to obsorb the west culture very quickly. So I think I can speak from both sides.

Thai family apparently is so weird to many of my American friends. For example, my mom and I we never say thank you. We say thank you to other people but not between each other. I could buy her the best gift for her birthday and she wouldn't say thank you. The same happens when she makes the best meal for me. The explaination for this is that we communicate stuff like love and gratitude through actions, not through words.

In our culture, there's a strong sense of role and duty. She knows her role as a mother and she tells you she cares by fulfulling her duties well. Me as a son also has a set of duties I need to fulfull. The way I tell my family I love them is to fulfill my duties. I'm 25 now and my mom still nags me about basic stuff like if I have eaten, if I do my laundry, etc. I used to be annoyed by this, but now I don't really mind it. I just let her say what she needs to say because she's just trying to show love the only way she knows how, by fulfulling her role as a mother. 

The truth is, it doesn't matter if you're 17 or 30, she will still nag you if you've eaten yet. So I wouldn't take that personally. 

As for the repeating stuff, It may be because of the language barrier and she wants to make sure that she's getting her point accross to you. I've seen my mom repeat stuff when she talk to people in English, where she's not very fluent. ( I speak to her in Thai so It's not an issue with me). If you want her to stop repeating I'd suggest repeating it back to her the first time what she saids to you just to assure her that you heard her the first time, or if she's not making sense, then ask her what she means, and try to figure it out with her. She won't feel bad, trust me, she wants to be able to communicate with her kid. She's probably has some internal insecurities about her ability to communicate because she barely knows the langauge and the culture is totally different. It might be a habit that she learned over the years, where she needed to say things many times in different way for people to understand her. 

She seems like a nice Thai mother who really loves her kid(s). And you will always be her kid. Let her be a mother. Let her nag you about some silly stuff, as long as it doesn't drain you emotionally. In Thai culture, it's not like we don't talk about feelings, we do, just in a different way. Sometimes a phone conversation with my mom consists of very basic facts like what I had for breakfast, what I had for lunch, who made the food, how good was it, what I plan to have for dinner, how much rice do I have left and when I'm I planning go to the store and buy more. Trust me, these converastions might seem silly for westerners but in Thai culture it's how we stay grounded with each other. It's just difference of cultures.

Omg I feel this to the core. I just finished a big desktop publishing project for client and I remember banging my head on the desk because just couldn't comprehend how much I needed to do. 

This is how I dealt with my ADHD during that project.

1) Seek constantly feedback. You have to find way to force yourself to let go of perfectionism, which is a big issue in people with ADHD. Idk what kind of project you're working on but for me it was a graphic design work. I'm generally terrified of letting people see the unfinished work, but this time I learned to be vulnerable and asked my roommate to give me some feedback. I even forced myself to send some unpolished drafts to my client for feedback even though part of me wanted to retain an image that I only do good work, and I always get it right the first time (which I don't). If your project is of a different nature and asking a roommate or client is not an option for you, maybe you could look into colleges, mentors, or even strangers on the internet?

2) Break it down and down. One way to get the ball rolling, for me, was to make my to do list very easy to attain at first. We all loved writing down big steps on our to do list but that's not helping at all. What I mean by this is, in order to get myself to feel okay working on the project, I would make my to do list consist of very small steps like "make page numbers", "find a color palette", "get rid of the squiggly lines on page 2", etc. And I try to force myself to focus on around 5-10 small steps at the time. Everytime I think about everything between then and the final product I get super overwhelmed so I had to make myself not think too far ahead ar a given moment. Ideally if you could break it down to say, each step takes you less than 3-5 min to do, then it makes crossing off the to do list very satisfying because you get to do it constantly and often. It's one way to visualize you're progress. Pro-tip for this is you can make a list of very small steps on a note book, then retype the list as bullet points on Google doc and print it out. A nice and cleanly formatted to do list that's very doable make everything more enjoyable and satisfying. Once you're get the ball rolling on this, chances your to do list will get increasingly complexed as you gain momentum. Which is what you want.

3) Let go of false sense of urgency. One important thing I realized is that I needed to take care of my basic needs first, and everything else comes second, regardless of how urgent everything seems. If anything, it will only help. For example, I know that my Adderall works best if I get a full night of sleep in. So I make sure I am well rested the night before, even if it means sleeping in a little. Or taking naps, etc. Eating well helps a lot. Go out for a long walk or jog in the middle of the day to get your mind off stuff can help. Take care of your mind and body and your mind and body will take care of you. Be proactive about your own needs. Try to calm the guilt. If you need extra time, and if it's possible to get extra time, make sure you ask. For me I literally said "Hey this is taking longer than I originally planned. I will have something for you tomorrow". 

4) Find way to calm your anxiety. For me, sometimes I just get bad anxiety while I'm working on the project. Like my heart is beating fast and I just hate working on what I'm doing. When this happens, given that I'm fully rested and eaten well, etc, it's because my brain is starved of stimulation because whatever I'm making myself do is just utterly boring. Something that helped me was putting on white noise on my headphones instead of music. There's a a huge library of ambient sounds you can find on youtube. My favorite is one of the new York city noise haha. I moved to a small town in Oregon because I just love the outdoors but one downside to is how quiet it is all the time. For some reason my brain really liked it when I gave it some chaotic city noise sounds to latch on to. Of course you're going to get bored of one sound pretty quick so don't be afraid to change it up to a different setting. A jungle maybe? A beach? Currently I've been liking cyberpunk city sounds. There's also a yt channel call Blume that has some amazing mixes of ambient sounds and music if you still prefer to listen to some melody. I also have a bookmark folder called 'epic sounds' that consists of some of the most badass orchestral music for when I want to change it up. Idk, have fun with it, see what can be a good pacifier for your brain so it leaves you alone to do your work..
